2750:
To cheap out means to deliberately choose a cheaper, lower-quality option at a moment when quality actually matters — and as a result, disappointing people, causing problems, or producing a poor outcome.

The key idea is not just that someone spent less money. It's that they spent less money when they shouldn't have. The savings came at a real cost — in quality, safety, relationships, or trust.

Think of it as: "saving money in the wrong place, at the wrong time, in a way that hurts the result."

"Cheap out" is a phrasal verb. Interestingly, "cheap" here is being used as a verb, not as an adjective. This surprises many learners because in everyday English, "cheap" is almost always an adjective ("a cheap phone," "that was cheap"). But in this phrasal verb, it acts as the action word.

It is an intransitive phrasal verb, which means it does not take a direct object immediately after it. You cannot say:

❌ "They cheaped out the wedding cake."

Instead, you use the preposition "on" to connect it to what was done cheaply:

✅ "They cheaped out on the wedding cake."

However, you can also use it without specifying what was done cheaply, and it still makes perfect sense:

✅ "Don't cheap out. It's your daughter's wedding."

SituationForm

In the present tense: "They always cheap out on important things."
In the past tense: "She cheaped out and bought the cheapest helmet available."
In the continuous form: "The company is cheaping out on customer support."
In the perfect form: "He has cheaped out on every vacation they've ever taken."

The past tense — "cheaped out" — is by far the most common form you will encounter.
The Tone and Feeling of the Phrase

"Cheap out" is almost always negative and critical. When you use it, you are expressing disapproval or disappointment. You are saying, in effect: "They should have spent more. They knew better. They chose poorly."

This is what separates "cheap out" from simply "saving money" or "being budget-conscious," which are neutral or even positive ideas. "Cheap out" carries a strong suggestion that the decision was wrong, selfish, or shortsighted.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "She saved money by cooking at home." → Neutral. Wise, even.
  • "She cheaped out and served instant noodles at her friend's birthday dinner." → Negative. Embarrassing. Inappropriate.

The difference is context. When the situation calls for quality, spending, or effort — and someone deliberately avoids it — that is when "cheap out" applies.
Real-Life Examples to Make It Stick

Example 1 — Construction:

"The builder cheaped out on the roof tiles, and now the whole ceiling leaks every time it rains."

The builder saved money by using low-quality tiles. But now there is a serious problem. The saving was not worth it.

Example 2 — Technology:

"The phone costs $1,200, but the company clearly cheaped out on the battery. It dies in four hours."

An expensive phone should have a good battery. The company saved money on a component where they really should not have. Buyers feel cheated.

Example 3 — A personal gift:

"He cheaped out on his wife's anniversary gift and bought her a $5 keychain."

The implication here is emotional, not just financial. He did not put thought or money into something that mattered to his wife. It feels disrespectful.

Example 4 — Food and hospitality:

"The restaurant cheaped out on the portion sizes. You pay €30 and get six tiny pieces of pasta."

The restaurant is cutting costs in a way that the customer clearly notices and resents.

Example 5 — Advice / warning:

"Do not cheap out on your running shoes. Bad shoes lead to knee injuries."

Here it is used as a direct warning. The speaker is saying: yes, good shoes cost more — but the cost of saving that money is too high.

Example 6 — Self-reflection:

"I cheaped out and bought the $20 umbrella. It turned inside-out in the first storm. Never again."

People use it about themselves too, when they regret a decision to save money.

It helps to know what this phrase does not mean, so you use it precisely.

It does not mean simply "to be poor." A person who cannot afford something is not "cheaping out." The phrase specifically suggests that the person had the ability to spend more but chose not to, usually for selfish or shortsighted reasons. There is a moral undertone of choice and responsibility.

It does not mean "to be frugal." Frugality is smart, deliberate, and sustainable money management. "Cheap out" is the opposite — it is cutting costs in a way that creates a worse outcome for yourself or others.

It does not always mean money. Sometimes "cheap out" can refer to cutting corners on effort or time, not just money. For example:

"He cheaped out on the presentation and just copy-pasted slides from last year."

He saved effort, not money. But the same idea applies — he gave less than the situation required.
The Difference Between "Cheap Out" and Similar Phrases

"Skimp on" is very similar and often interchangeable. "They skimped on the butter" means they used less butter than they should have. The difference is subtle: "skimp on" often focuses on using too little of something, while "cheap out" focuses more broadly on making a cheaper choice overall.

"Cut corners" is also related, but it focuses more on skipping steps in a process to save time or money. A builder who cuts corners skips safety checks. "Cheap out" focuses more on choosing lower quality materials or options.

"Penny-pinching" describes a personality trait — a person who is always, obsessively careful about spending money, even in small amounts. "Cheap out" describes a specific action in a specific moment, not a general personality.
Register: When and Where Is This Phrase Used?

"Cheap out" is informal and colloquial. You will hear it in:

  • Casual conversation between friends
  • Online product reviews ("The brand cheaped out on the stitching")
  • Gaming and tech forums ("They really cheaped out on the GPU this generation")
  • Social media comments
  • YouTube videos reviewing products

You would not use it in formal writing, academic essays, legal documents, or professional business reports. In those contexts, you would say something like "the company prioritized cost reduction over quality" or "insufficient investment in materials."
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

"Cheap out (on something)" = to deliberately choose a lower-quality, lower-cost option in a situation where quality matters — resulting in disappointment, failure, or a worse outcome.

  • It is informal and negative.
  • It implies a choice, not a lack of money.
  • It is followed by "on" when specifying what was done cheaply.
  • The past tense "cheaped out" is the most common form.
  • It criticizes someone (or yourself) for saving money at the wrong moment, in the wrong way.

"Don't cheap out on the things that matter."
That one sentence captures the entire soul of this phrasal verb.
2751:
A cheapskate is a person who strongly dislikes spending money — not because they can't afford it, but because they simply refuse to part with it, even when they clearly should.

The key phrase is "even when they clearly should." A cheapskate doesn't just avoid unnecessary spending. They avoid spending in situations where most people consider it normal, fair, or expected — like splitting a dinner bill honestly, tipping a waiter for good service, or buying a thoughtful gift for a close friend. Their stinginess often inconveniences, embarrasses, or burdens the people around them.

Calling someone a cheapskate is never a compliment. It implies that the person isn't just careful with money — they're petty and selfish about it. The word suggests a kind of small-mindedness: they let their reluctance to spend money override what's fair, kind, or socially appropriate. People who are called cheapskates are generally seen as frustrating and disrespectful, not admirable.

The clearest way to understand the word is through real behavior. Here are classic examples:

  • At a restaurant with friends, the cheapskate calculates their exact share of the bill down to the last rupee — while everyone else rounds up generously.
  • They give a cheap, inadequate gift for a big occasion (a wedding, a graduation) to save money.
  • They refuse to tip service workers, even when the service was excellent.
  • They borrow money or things from others and "forget" to return or repay.
  • In a group where everyone contributes to a shared expense — a farewell gift, a party, a trip — the cheapskate finds a reason not to contribute, or contributes far less than their fair share.

Notice a pattern: in almost every case, the cheapskate's behavior costs someone else — either in money, effort, or goodwill. That is the heart of why we find cheapskates frustrating. It's not just that they're saving money for themselves; it's that they're often doing it at others' expense.
A cheapskate is NOT someone who is poor

This distinction matters. A cheapskate is not someone who avoids spending because they genuinely cannot afford something. If a person is broke or on a tight budget, we don't call them a cheapskate — that would be unfair and unkind.

A cheapskate is someone who has the money but chooses not to spend it, particularly in social situations where spending is the fair and expected thing to do. The refusal is a choice, not a necessity.
The most important distinction: cheapskate vs. frugal/thrifty

Understanding this difference is essential to truly understanding the word.

A frugal or thrifty person is careful and smart about money. They avoid waste, hunt for good deals, and make sensible financial decisions. This is a positive quality — we admire and respect frugal people. Being frugal is wise.

A cheapskate takes it too far. Their money-consciousness crosses a line into selfishness and social unfairness. This is a negative quality — we are frustrated with cheapskates.

The difference is not simply about how little you spend. It's about fairness, generosity, and your effect on others.

A simple contrast:

  • Buying a no-brand version of a product to save money → frugal.
  • Refusing to contribute to a colleague's farewell gift when everyone else is chipping in → cheapskate.
  • Cooking at home instead of eating out → frugal.
  • Going out with friends, ordering the most expensive item on the menu, and then claiming you only have enough to pay for your own food → cheapskate.

The frugal person is making sensible personal choices. The cheapskate is imposing their money anxiety on other people.
How it compares to similar words

Several words are close in meaning to cheapskate, but each has a slightly different shade:

Stingy — Very similar. A stingy person is unwilling to give or spend. The word focuses more on the emotional refusal to be generous. You can be stingy with money, but also with praise, time, or affection. "Stingy" is slightly more formal than "cheapskate."

Miser — A much stronger word. A miser is obsessed with accumulating and protecting money to an extreme, almost pathological degree. The word suggests that money-hoarding defines and controls the person's entire life. All cheapskates are a little miserly, but a true miser is a far more severe case.

Penny-pincher — Nearly identical to cheapskate. It emphasizes obsessive attention to even the tiniest amounts of money — counting every single penny.

Tightwad — Another informal synonym for cheapskate. It suggests the person holds onto their money so "tightly" that nothing can get out of their grip.

Of all these words, cheapskate is the most commonly used in everyday conversation. It carries a clear social judgment: not just that someone is careful with money, but that their behavior is socially wrong — unfair to others, petty, and ungenerous.
Can you call yourself a cheapskate?

Yes, and people do it all the time — humorously. When you call yourself a cheapskate, it softens the criticism into a self-aware, self-deprecating joke. You're acknowledging your own reluctance to spend money in a lighthearted way.

For example: "I walked forty minutes instead of taking a cab. I know, I'm such a cheapskate."

When used this way, it's almost charming — you're laughing at yourself.

But when you call someone else a cheapskate, it is almost always a genuine criticism, not a joke.

• "Don't be a cheapskate — just leave a proper tip!"
  • "He's such a cheapskate that he reuses disposable plates."
  • "She's the office cheapskate — she never contributes when we order food together."
  • "My cousin is a total cheapskate; he gave me a used book as a birthday gift and didn't even bother to remove the old name from the cover."
  • "I felt like a cheapskate when I realized everyone else had bought the host a proper gift and I'd shown up empty-handed."
  • "Stop being a cheapskate and just buy a decent pair of shoes — you've been wearing those for eight years."

A cheapskate is someone who has money but refuses to spend it even when spending is fair, kind, or expected — and whose tightfistedness inconveniences or burdens the people around them. It is always used as a criticism, and it describes a character flaw, not a financial situation.
2752:
To check means to look at something carefully to make sure it is correct, safe, true, or in good condition. This is the central idea behind almost everything this word does.

Think of it this way: when you check something, you are paying deliberate, focused attention to it — not just glancing at it, but actively verifying it.

1. To Examine or Verify

This is the most common use. You look at something carefully to confirm whether it is correct, accurate, or as expected.

  • Check your answers before submitting the exam. (Look carefully to see if they're right.)
  • The doctor checked the patient's blood pressure. (Examined it to know the value.)
  • Can you check if the door is locked? (Verify whether the door is locked or not.)

The key feeling here is: you are not sure about something, so you go and find out by looking at it closely.

You can check a fact, check a document, check your work, check the weather, check your phone — in every case, you are directing your attention to something to confirm a specific detail about it.

2. To Stop or Control Something

Here, check means to slow down, restrain, or bring something under control — usually something that was moving forward, growing, or getting out of hand.

  • The medicine helped check the spread of the infection. (Stopped it from spreading further.)
  • She checked her anger and spoke calmly. (Held back her anger; controlled it.)
  • The government took steps to check inflation. (Control and reduce it.)

Think of it as putting a hand up in front of something to stop it. The idea is: something was growing or moving, and you applied force to block or limit it.

3. To Mark Something as Done

In everyday tasks and lists, check means to place a mark (✓) next to something to show it has been done, confirmed, or noticed.

  • Check the boxes that apply to you.
  • I checked off every item on my to-do list.

This meaning comes from the physical action of drawing a checkmark. Over time, "to check" came to mean the act itself — acknowledging that something is complete or confirmed.
Important Phrasal Verbs (Combinations with Other Words)

"Check" combines with small words to create meanings that are distinct and very commonly used. These are essential to know.

Check in

To officially register your arrival at a place — typically a hotel, airport, hospital, or event.

  • We checked in at the hotel at 3 PM. (Went to the reception, gave our name, received our room key.)
  • Passengers must check in one hour before the flight.

It can also mean to make brief contact with someone to update them or see how they are:

  • My manager checks in with me every Monday. (Has a short conversation to see how things are going.)

Check out

This has two very different uses:

1. To leave officially (the opposite of checking in):

  • We checked out of the hotel in the morning. (Handed over the key, paid, and left.)
  • At the supermarket, she went to the checkout counter. (The place where you pay and leave.)

2. To borrow something officially, like from a library:

  • He checked out three books from the library. (Registered them as borrowed.)

3. Informally, to look at something with interest:

  • Check out that view! (Look at it — it's worth seeing!)
  • I'll check out that new restaurant. (I'll go and try it / explore it.)

Check on

To go and see how someone or something is doing — usually out of care or responsibility.

  • The nurse checked on the patient every hour. (Visited briefly to see if everything was okay.)
  • Can you check on the baby while I cook? (Look in on the baby to make sure all is well.)

Check up on

Similar to "check on," but with a slightly stronger sense of monitoring or making sure someone is doing what they should be doing.

  • Her parents called to check up on her.
  • The supervisor checked up on the team's progress. (Looked into how the work was going — with an implication of oversight.)

Check with

To ask someone to confirm or get their approval before doing something.

  • Before I make the booking, let me check with my wife. (Confirm with her that she agrees.)
  • Check with the doctor before taking this medicine. (Ask the doctor and get their opinion first.)

Check yourself

To pause and reconsider your own actions, words, or behavior — to catch yourself before you do or say something you might regret.

  • He was about to say something rude, but he checked himself. (Stopped himself in time.)

Check vs. Look:
When you just look at something, it is passive — your eyes fall on it. When you check something, it is active and purposeful — you are looking for something specific, trying to confirm or rule out something.

  • She looked at the report. (Her eyes were on it.)
  • She checked the report. (She examined it to verify that it was accurate, complete, or correct.)

Check vs. Inspect:
Both mean examining carefully, but inspect tends to be more formal and thorough — like an official going through something systematically. Check is more everyday and general. You check your email; a government official inspects a factory.

Check vs. Control (in the "stop/restrain" meaning):
Control suggests ongoing management. Check in this sense is more like applying a sudden restraint — you interrupt or limit something that was building up or moving.
The Common Thread Across All Meanings

No matter how "check" is used, there is always one underlying idea: conscious, deliberate attention being applied to something. Whether you are verifying a fact, stopping a process, marking a list, or registering at a hotel — in each case, something is being acknowledged, confirmed, or brought under control through intentional action.

This is why "check" feels like such an active, purposeful word. It is never accidental or passive. When you check something, you are doing it on purpose.
A Few Natural Examples Across Contexts

• Always check your work before you hand it in. — Verify it for mistakes.
  • The treatment helped check the disease. — Stopped it from spreading.
  • Check that option if you agree. — Mark it with a checkmark.
  • Did you check in for your flight? — Register your arrival at the airport.
  • I'll check on the kids in a minute. — Go see how they are.
  • Let me check with the team first. — Confirm with them before deciding.
  • He had to check himself from laughing. — Hold himself back.
  • Check out this article — it's fascinating. — Look at / read this.

By the time you have absorbed these meanings and examples, you have a complete and accurate picture of what the verb "check" does in English — in formal writing, casual speech, and everything in between.
2753: The word checkered as an adjective has two distinct meanings — one literal and one figurative. Both are important and widely used in English. Once you understand both, you will recognize this word everywhere.
The Literal Meaning — A Visual Pattern

In its most direct sense, "checkered" describes something that has a pattern of alternating squares in two colors — usually black and white — arranged in a grid, much like a chessboard or a checkerboard.

Examples:

  • A checkered tablecloth at a pizza restaurant has red and white squares.
  • A checkered floor in a kitchen has black and white tiles.
  • The famous racing flag waved at the end of a car race is called a checkered flag — it is white and black squares.

The key idea here is simple: a repeating pattern of two alternating colors in square shapes. If you can picture a chessboard, you can picture something that is checkered.
The Figurative Meaning — A Mixed History

This is the more commonly used meaning in everyday English, and it is the one you will encounter most often. Here, "checkered" is used to describe a person's life, career, past, or history that has had both good periods and bad periods — a mix of highs and lows, successes and failures, achievements and mistakes.

The logic behind this is beautiful: just as a checkered pattern alternates between dark and light squares, a "checkered" life alternates between dark times (failures, mistakes, troubles) and bright times (successes, achievements). It is never all one thing.

The most important nuance: When people use "checkered" in this figurative sense, they usually mean the person or thing has had some notable problems, controversies, or moral failures — not just ordinary ups and downs. It leans slightly toward the negative. It is not a neutral or purely positive word. Calling something "checkered" is a polite but honest way of saying: "There have been some real problems here, alongside the good things."

Examples:

  • "He had a checkered past." → He did some questionable or problematic things earlier in his life, though perhaps he has changed.
  • "The company has a checkered history." → The company has had both periods of success and periods of scandal, failure, or wrongdoing.
  • "She had a checkered career in politics." → Her political career saw some achievements, but also controversies, defeats, or scandals.

It does not mean simply "interesting" or "varied." It carries the specific implication of moral, professional, or personal inconsistency — some darkness mixed into the story. If someone only had a brilliant, flawless career, you would never call it "checkered." The word would feel wrong and out of place.

These are the phrases you will most frequently see "checkered" used in:

  • A checkered past — The most common phrase. A personal history that includes mistakes, wrongdoing, or troubled episodes.
  • A checkered career — A professional life with notable highs but also significant lows or controversies.
  • A checkered history — Used for organizations, institutions, countries, or relationships that have gone through both good and troubled periods.
  • A checkered record — Someone's track record that shows inconsistency, both impressive and troubling results.
  • The checkered flag — The literal black-and-white flag used in motor racing to signal the end of a race.
A Simple Way to Always Remember Both Meanings

Think of a chessboard. Now hold that image in your mind.

Literal → If something looks like a chessboard (alternating squares of two colors), it is checkered.

Figurative → If someone's life or career looks like a chessboard — dark squares (bad times) and light squares (good times) alternating throughout — it is checkered. And because the dark squares are hard to ignore, the word carries a hint of warning or caution.

"Checkered" is a standard, neutral-to-slightly-formal word. It is not slang. It is not rude. It is, however, honest. When used figuratively, it is often a diplomatic way of acknowledging something negative without being harsh or blunt. A journalist might write "the organization has a checkered history" instead of directly saying "the organization has done some terrible things." It softens the criticism while still being truthful.

Once you internalize the image of a chessboard — alternating dark and light — you have the entire word in your grasp, both in what it looks like and what it means about a person or thing's story.
2754:
"Cheeky" describes a person or behavior that is a little bold, slightly disrespectful, or pushes a boundary — but in a playful, light-hearted way that makes it hard to stay angry about.

The key thing that separates "cheeky" from just being "rude" is this: there is always a sense of fun, mischief, or charm underneath it. The person doing the cheeky thing often does it with a sly grin or a wink. And the person on the receiving end usually ends up half-amused, even if they're pretending to be annoyed.

Think of it as standing right at the edge of the line between acceptable and unacceptable — and dancing on that edge with a smile.
What Does It Actually Look Like?

Here are some real-life situations that capture "cheeky" perfectly:

Example 1: A child has just been told "no more sweets." Thirty seconds later, he walks back in, gives his mother his biggest, most innocent smile, and quietly places one more sweet in his mouth while looking her right in the eye. That child is being cheeky. He knows he's crossing a line. He's doing it anyway. And he's doing it with enough charm that his mother might actually laugh despite herself.

Example 2: You're at lunch with a friend. Your chips (fries) are sitting on the table. Without asking, your friend reaches over, steals a handful, and gives you a cheeky smile as if to say, "Yeah, I just did that." That's cheeky. It's a tiny bit rude, but it's done with such easy confidence and playfulness that it's more funny than offensive.

Example 3: A new employee, on only his second week at work, jokingly asks his boss, "So when's my first raise?" with a big grin. The boss raises an eyebrow. The employee is being cheeky — a little bold and presumptuous, but not in a way that reads as genuinely disrespectful. It might actually make the boss smile.

Example 4: At a party, someone turns to a friend on their birthday and says, "You're 30 now? You're practically ancient!" with a big laugh. Cheeky. A bit much, slightly rude — but said in a way that's clearly affectionate.

In all these cases, notice: the behavior is slightly over the line. But the spirit behind it is warm, playful, or amusing. That combination is the heart of "cheeky."

When someone calls a person or action "cheeky," they are usually not truly angry. The word itself signals that the speaker finds the situation at least a little amusing, even if they're shaking their head. There's a kind of warmth baked into the word.

Compare how these two sentences feel:

  • "That was rude." → Genuinely bothered. No warmth.
  • "That was a bit cheeky!" → Mildly exasperated, but secretly charmed.

If you call something cheeky, you are almost automatically softening the criticism. You're saying: "You stepped out of line — but not in a way I can stay mad about."
Who or What Can Be Cheeky?

People can be cheeky — especially children, who are described this way very often. A cheeky child is a mischievous, spirited, slightly sassy one. It's usually said with great affection.

But remarks, questions, smiles, and requests can also be cheeky:

  • A cheeky question is one that is a little too bold or forward for the situation.
  • A cheeky grin is a sly, knowing smile worn by someone who knows they're being naughty.
  • A cheeky request is one that the person asking knows is a bit much to ask.

Even certain actions can be described as cheeky — sneaking something, saying something you probably shouldn't have, taking a liberty you weren't given.
Where "Cheeky" Sits on the Scale of Boldness

It helps to understand where "cheeky" falls among similar words:

  • Shy / timid → the complete opposite of cheeky
  • Playful → close, but playful doesn't involve crossing a line
  • Cheeky → playful + slightly over the line + charming about it
  • Bold / brazen → more serious; no longer cute or funny
  • Rude / insolent → genuinely disrespectful, no warmth left at all

Cheeky lives in that sweet spot that is too bold to be fully innocent, but too charming to be truly offensive. The moment the charm disappears, the behavior stops being cheeky and becomes something harsher.

Yes, absolutely — and quite often it is. When adults say "Oh, she's a cheeky one!" about a child, they usually mean it fondly. It suggests spirit, confidence, and wit. A cheeky person tends to be seen as lively and entertaining, someone who makes situations more fun.

Even when someone says "That was a bit cheeky of you," in a reproving tone, there is often an undercurrent of "...but I kind of respect the nerve."

However, context matters. If someone has genuinely overstepped and there is real irritation, "cheeky" can be used critically — as in, "I thought that was rather cheeky of him, honestly." But even then, the word choice signals that the speaker considers it more of an impertinence than a serious offense.
How "Cheeky" Is Different from Similar Words

Cheeky vs. Rude:
Rude has no warmth or playfulness. If someone is rude, they are being genuinely disrespectful or offensive. Cheeky always has that light, mischievous quality that keeps it out of truly offensive territory.

Cheeky vs. Mischievous:
Mischievous focuses on causing trouble or playing tricks — it's about what someone does. Cheeky is more about attitude — the bold, slightly disrespectful confidence someone carries, often with a grin.

Cheeky vs. Sassy:
These are very similar. "Sassy" is used more in American English and often implies a sharper, wittier kind of backtalk — especially from someone in a less powerful position (like a child talking back). "Cheeky" is the more British and Australian word and feels slightly more gentle and playful.

Cheeky vs. Impudent:
"Impudent" is more formal and more negative. An impudent person shows a lack of respect in a way that is more openly offensive. Cheeky is lighter — it still has that saving grace of charm.
A Note on Where This Word Is Most Used

"Cheeky" is primarily a British and Australian English word. If you are reading British novels, watching British TV shows, or talking with British or Australian people, you will encounter it often. While people in other English-speaking countries understand it, they are less likely to use it naturally in everyday speech.

Cheeky = slightly bold, a little disrespectful, pushing a boundary just past where it should be — but done with such playful confidence and charm that it is more amusing than offensive. The behavior is naughty, but lightly so. The person doing it usually knows it, and often wears a sly grin to go with it. And the person on the receiving end might shake their head — but is probably smiling underneath.

If you ever see someone do something a little too bold, a little too presumptuous, with a sparkle in their eye and no real malice in their heart — that is cheeky.
2755:
To cheese someone off means to annoy, irritate, or frustrate someone — to make them feel fed up or displeased. When you cheese someone off, you do something that gets under their skin and puts them in a bad mood.

Think of it this way: imagine someone keeps tapping their pen on the desk during a quiet meeting. That repetitive, unnecessary action cheeses people off — it irritates them even if it seems like a small thing.

The annoyance expressed by this idiom sits at a mild to moderate level on the anger scale. It is:

  • Stronger than being slightly bothered or mildly uncomfortable.
  • Weaker than being furious, outraged, or livid.

It is the kind of irritation you feel when someone is being inconsiderate, unfair, or just plain difficult — not enough to make you explode, but enough to genuinely bother you.

This idiom appears in two closely related forms, and you must understand both:

1. As an active verb phrase — "cheese someone off"

Here, a person or situation is the cause of the annoyance, and someone else is the receiver of that annoyance.

Structure: Subject + cheese(s)/cheesed + object + off

  • "His constant interruptions cheese me off."
  • "That unfair decision really cheesed everyone off."
  • "Stop doing that — you're cheesing me off!"

2. As an adjective — "cheesed off"

Here, the focus is on the person who feels the annoyance. You describe their emotional state.

Structure: Subject + be/feel + cheesed off

  • "I am cheesed off about what happened."
  • "She looked completely cheesed off after the meeting."
  • "He's been cheesed off all day because his flight was cancelled."

Both forms come from the same root idea, but one is about the action of annoying someone, and the other describes the state of being annoyed.

This idiom is informal and colloquial. You would use it in:

  • Casual conversation with friends and family.
  • Informal writing like texts, social media, or personal blogs.

You would not typically use it in:

  • Professional emails or workplace reports.
  • Academic writing or formal speeches.
  • Polite conversation with someone you don't know well.

"Cheese someone off" is most commonly heard in British English. It has been part of British informal speech since at least the mid-20th century, and records of "cheesed off" go back to around the 1940s, when British soldiers used it to mean feeling bored, discontented, or fed up.

It is understood in American English as well, but Americans more typically use alternatives like:

  • Tick someone off
  • Tee someone off
  • Bug someone
  • Get on someone's nerves
  • Drive someone up the wall

Almost anything can cheese someone off — a person, a situation, a rule, a habit, or an event. Here are realistic examples:

  • A person: "My neighbour's loud music at midnight really cheeses me off."
  • A situation: "Waiting in a long queue for something that takes two minutes cheeses people off."
  • A habit: "It cheeses her off when people don't say thank you."
  • A rule or decision: "The new parking policy has cheesed off a lot of residents."

When someone uses this idiom, the tone is usually one of genuine but controlled frustration. It often carries a slight edge of complaint — the speaker wants you to know they are not happy, but they are not screaming either.

It can also be used with a hint of humour, especially in British speech, where understatement and mild sarcasm are common. For example:

  • "Oh, that new update has well and truly cheesed me off." — said with a sigh and a slight eye-roll.

Mistake 1: Using it in formal contexts.
Saying "Your conduct has cheesed off the management" in a professional letter would sound strange and unprofessional. Stick to formal synonyms like irritated, frustrated, or displeased in formal writing.

Mistake 2: Confusing intensity.
Don't use it to describe extreme rage. If someone is absolutely furious, cheesed off would be an understatement. It covers everyday irritation, not deep anger.

Mistake 3: Wrong word order.
The object (the person being annoyed) must come between "cheese" and "off" — or the word "off" must follow naturally.

  • ✅ "It cheesed me off."
  • ✅ "That really cheeses her off."
  • ❌ "It cheesed off me." ← This sounds unnatural when a pronoun is used.

However, when the object is a noun (not a pronoun), both orders can work:

  • ✅ "It cheesed the whole team off."
  • ✅ "It cheesed off the whole team."

ElementDetail

To put it all together simply: "cheese someone off" means to annoy or irritate someone. It is an informal British idiom of moderate emotional intensity — somewhere between mildly bothered and genuinely angry. It works both as an active verb ("you're cheesing me off") and as a descriptive phrase ("I'm cheesed off"). Use it in casual, everyday speech — never in formal writing. It's a vivid, expressive little idiom that perfectly captures that relatable feeling of being needlessly frustrated by something or someone.
2756: Cheeseparing describes someone who is extremely and pettily unwilling to spend money or share resources — even when they can afford to be more generous. It means being so tight with money that it comes across as mean-spirited and small-minded, not just careful.

This is the most important thing to understand about "cheeseparing": it is not a neutral word. It is a disapproving, slightly contemptuous word. When you call someone or something cheeseparing, you are not simply observing that they are careful with money — you are criticizing them for it. You are saying their stinginess is petty and unbecoming.

Think of it like this: the word carries a quiet sneer inside it.
The crucial difference: cheeseparing vs. frugal vs. thrifty

This is where many learners get confused, so pay close attention.

  • Frugal and thrifty are generally positive words. They describe someone who is sensibly careful with money — avoiding waste, living within their means, making smart choices. We admire a frugal person.
  • Cheeseparing is negative. It describes someone whose carefulness with money has crossed a line into something mean, petty, and unpleasant — especially when they are not even poor and have no good reason to be so stingy.

A frugal person buys what they need and avoids unnecessary waste. A cheeseparing person pinches pennies even when it hurts others, skimps when they shouldn't, and prioritizes saving a small amount of money over being decent or fair.

A simple way to remember: frugality is a virtue; cheeseparing is a vice.
What can be described as cheeseparing?

The adjective can be attached to several kinds of things:

A person:

"He was a cheeseparing old miser who refused to heat his own home in winter."

Behavior or habits:

"Her cheeseparing ways meant she would reuse a teabag three times before throwing it away."

A decision, policy, or approach:

"The government's cheeseparing cuts to the school budget left children without basic supplies."
"The cheeseparing attitude of the management meant employees rarely received fair pay rises."

So it is not only used to describe individual people — it can describe an approach, a mindset, or a policy that reflects this kind of petty stinginess.

These sentences will help you see the word in action:

  • "The landlord's cheeseparing refusal to fix the heating made the winter miserable for his tenants."
  • "Despite being a millionaire, he had a reputation for cheeseparing behavior — he once argued over a small invoice for twenty minutes."
  • "The charity complained that the cheeseparing donation from the corporation barely covered a week's expenses."
  • "She grew up in a cheeseparing household where nothing was ever spent on pleasure or comfort."

In every case, notice that the stinginess feels unnecessary and unkind — that is the heart of the word.
Words that are similar — and how cheeseparing sits among them

There is a whole family of words for stinginess, each with slightly different shades:

  • Stingy — the most common, everyday word for unwillingness to spend or give. Cheeseparing is stronger and more literary.
  • Miserly — describes someone obsessed with hoarding money, like a miser. Very similar to cheeseparing, but "miserly" suggests a deeper, almost pathological obsession with money.
  • Penny-pinching — informal and vivid; focuses on the idea of obsessing over tiny amounts of money. Very close to cheeseparing.
  • Tight-fisted / close-fisted — informal ways of saying someone holds their money tightly and will not let it go.
  • Parsimonious — a formal, even academic word for extreme reluctance to spend. It is less emotionally charged than cheeseparing.
  • Mean (British English especially) — in British usage, "mean" often simply means stingy or ungenerous, and is close in feeling to cheeseparing.

Among all of these, cheeseparing stands out for its strong sense of pettiness — the implication that the stinginess is not just about amounts of money, but about a small-minded, ungenerous character.
The register: when and where is this word used?

"Cheeseparing" is slightly old-fashioned and literary in flavor. You are more likely to encounter it in:

  • British English than American English
  • Written texts, journalism, and formal speech rather than casual conversation
  • Literature, criticism, or commentary where the writer wants to convey disapproval with a bit of edge

It is not a word you would use in everyday casual chat — you would more likely say "stingy" or "tight-fisted" there. But in writing, or in formal speech, cheeseparing adds a crisp, expressive quality that plain words like "stingy" sometimes lack.
If you need to nail it in one sentence: cheeseparing means so petty and mean with money or resources that it is contemptible — not careful, but shamefully and unnecessarily tight-fisted.
2757: A chemise is a simple, loose, straight-hanging garment for the body — one with almost no shaping, no tight waistline, no structural complexity. Think of a soft tube of fabric that drapes straight down from the shoulders. That simplicity is what defines it.

A chemise is typically:

  • Sleeveless, or with very thin shoulder straps
  • Straight-cut — it doesn't nip in at the waist or flare out dramatically at the hips; it just falls in a clean, simple line
  • Short to medium in length — usually ending somewhere between mid-thigh and the knee, though this varies
  • Made of light, soft fabric — commonly silk, satin, cotton, linen, or lace

The overall impression is of something effortless and unstructured. It's the opposite of a sculpted, tailored garment.

The word "chemise" is used in two related but distinct contexts today:

1. As a lingerie or sleepwear item

This is the most common modern use. A chemise in this sense is a short, slip-like garment worn either to sleep in or as intimate/boudoir wear. It's similar to a nightgown but shorter and more delicate. It typically has thin spaghetti straps, a low neckline, and is made of silky or lacy fabric. It sits loosely on the body and is meant to be both comfortable and aesthetically appealing.

If you've ever seen a character in a film wearing a sleek, silky slip to bed — that's a chemise.

2. As a style of dress (outerwear)

A chemise can also refer to a particular style of women's dress — often called a "chemise dress" — that mimics the same straight, loose, unstructured silhouette. It has no defined waist. It just hangs from the shoulders in a relaxed, column-like shape. This style was especially fashionable in the 1920s and again in the late 1950s–60s, when fashion moved away from the cinched waists of the previous decade toward something freer and simpler.
Historical background (what it used to mean)

For most of European history — roughly from the Middle Ages through the 1800s — a chemise was the basic undergarment worn directly against the skin, by both men and women. It was essentially a loose, long shirt made of linen or cotton. People wore it under everything else: under corsets, under gowns, under breeches.

It served a very practical purpose: since outer garments were expensive and hard to wash, the chemise absorbed sweat and body oils and was washed regularly instead. It was the foundation of any outfit.

Over time, as undergarments became more specialized and diversified, the word "chemise" narrowed in meaning and eventually came to refer mostly to women's garments — specifically the lingerie/sleepwear item or the loose dress style.
How it differs from similar garments

These are items people often confuse with a chemise:

  • Camisole ("cami"): A camisole is shorter — it covers just the torso and typically ends at or near the hip. A chemise is longer, covering more of the body (down to the mid-thigh or beyond).
  • Slip: A slip is also a smooth, lightweight undergarment worn under a dress or skirt to prevent the outer fabric from clinging to the body. A chemise can be worn as a standalone garment (as sleepwear or a dress), while a slip is usually purely a layering piece worn invisibly beneath something else.
  • Nightgown: A nightgown is longer — typically reaching the knee, the calf, or even the ankle. A chemise is shorter and tends to feel more intimate or fashion-forward than a standard nightgown.
  • Shift dress: A "shift" and a "chemise dress" are very nearly the same thing. Both are straight, loose, unstructured dresses. "Shift" is more commonly used in fashion and everyday conversation when talking about outerwear; "chemise" is the older, more traditional term and is also used in lingerie contexts.

A chemise is a simple, loose, straight-falling garment — no waist definition, no fuss. In everyday modern life, you'll most often encounter the word in one of two situations: describing a piece of silk or satin sleepwear/lingerie (short, slip-like, worn to bed or as intimate wear), or describing a relaxed, column-shaped dress with no fitted waist. Both uses share the same essence: lightness, simplicity, and a garment that drapes freely rather than sculpting the body.
2758:
Chemotherapy is a medical treatment that uses powerful chemical drugs to destroy or stop the growth of cancer cells in the body.

But to truly understand the word, you need to understand the problem it's trying to solve.

Cancer is not an outside invader like a virus or bacteria. It is your own body's cells gone rogue — cells that have lost the ability to stop dividing and start multiplying out of control, forming tumours, invading tissues, and spreading. Because cancer cells are your own cells, you can't simply take a drug that targets "foreign things." You need something powerful enough to attack cells that are a part of you, but that are misbehaving.

This is the central challenge — and the reason chemotherapy is both lifesaving and brutal.

Most cells in your body divide and grow at a controlled pace. Cancer cells divide rapidly and relentlessly — much faster than most healthy cells. Chemotherapy drugs exploit this difference.

These drugs interfere with a cell's ability to divide and copy itself. They might damage the cell's DNA directly, block the chemical processes needed for cell division, or destroy the machinery a cell uses to split into two. When a cell can't divide properly, it dies.

Because cancer cells are dividing so fast, they are far more likely to be caught in the act by these drugs — and therefore more likely to be killed.

Here is the key limitation: chemotherapy drugs aren't perfectly precise. They cannot perfectly distinguish between a cancer cell and a healthy one. They simply target any rapidly dividing cell.

Your body has several types of normal, healthy cells that also divide quickly:

  • Hair follicle cells — which is why hair falls out
  • Cells lining the mouth, stomach, and intestines — which causes mouth sores, nausea, and vomiting
  • Bone marrow cells — which produce blood cells; when these are damaged, the patient becomes anaemic (low red blood cells), has a weakened immune system (low white blood cells), and bleeds or bruises easily (low platelets)

So when someone on chemotherapy loses their hair, feels constantly nauseated, or gets sick easily — it's not a coincidence or an allergic reaction. It is the predictable, logical consequence of a treatment that hits fast-dividing cells indiscriminately.

Chemotherapy can enter the body in several ways:

  • Intravenous (IV) — directly into a vein through a drip or a port. This is the most common method and allows the drug to travel through the bloodstream to reach cancer cells anywhere in the body.
  • Oral — as pills or capsules swallowed by mouth.
  • Injection — directly into a muscle or under the skin.
  • Topical — as a cream applied to the skin, used for certain skin cancers.
  • Intrathecal — injected directly into the spinal fluid, for cancers affecting the brain or nervous system.

Most chemotherapy is given in cycles — a period of treatment, then a rest period, then treatment again. The rest period is crucial: it gives healthy cells time to recover before the next round of drugs hits.

Chemotherapy isn't always given with the same goal in mind. Depending on the situation, it can be:

  1. Curative — the goal is to completely eliminate the cancer and achieve a permanent cure.
  2. Adjuvant chemotherapy — given after surgery or radiation to kill any cancer cells that may have been left behind but are too small to detect.
  3. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy — given before surgery to shrink a tumour, making it easier (or possible) to operate.
  4. Palliative chemotherapy — when a cure is no longer realistic, chemotherapy can still shrink tumours, slow the cancer's spread, and relieve symptoms, improving a patient's quality of life and possibly extending it.

There isn't just one chemotherapy drug — there are many, and they work in different ways. They are grouped into classes:

  • Alkylating agents — directly damage the DNA inside cancer cells, preventing them from copying themselves (e.g., cyclophosphamide).
  • Antimetabolites — mimic the building blocks of DNA or RNA, sneaking into the cell and disrupting its ability to replicate (e.g., methotrexate, 5-fluorouracil).
  • Topoisomerase inhibitors — block an enzyme the cell needs to unwind and copy its DNA.
  • Mitotic inhibitors — interfere with the physical process of a cell splitting into two (e.g., taxanes like paclitaxel, and vinca alkaloids like vincristine).
  • Anti-tumour antibiotics — despite the name, these are not used for infections; they interfere with the enzymes involved in DNA replication inside tumour cells.

In practice, doctors often combine drugs from different classes — this is called combination chemotherapy — because hitting the cancer from multiple angles at once makes it harder for cancer cells to survive or develop resistance.

Chemotherapy is one of several major ways to treat cancer. Understanding how it differs from the others helps place it clearly:

  • Surgery physically removes the tumour from the body. It works locally, but can't reach cancer cells that have already spread.
  • Radiation therapy uses high-energy rays (like X-rays) aimed at a specific spot to destroy cancer cells there. Also local.
  • Chemotherapy is systemic — it travels through the entire bloodstream, reaching cancer cells anywhere in the body. This is its great strength when cancer has spread to multiple locations (called metastasis).
  • Targeted therapy uses drugs designed to attack very specific proteins or mutations found in certain cancer cells, making it more precise and often with fewer side effects than traditional chemo.
  • Immunotherapy works differently altogether — instead of attacking the cancer directly, it trains or enhances the body's own immune system to recognise and destroy cancer cells.

Chemotherapy is often used alongside these other treatments, not just alone.
The word in everyday vs. strict usage

In the broadest technical sense, "chemotherapy" means treatment of any disease using chemical substances — which would technically include antibiotics. But in modern medicine and in everyday life, the word has narrowed almost entirely to mean cancer treatment using cytotoxic (cell-killing) drugs. When a doctor, a news article, or a person says "chemotherapy" or "chemo," they mean cancer treatment. That narrower meaning is the standard one you will encounter in virtually every context.

Chemotherapy is a powerful, systemic cancer treatment that works by introducing chemical drugs into the body to interfere with the rapid division of cancer cells, ultimately killing them. Because it targets fast-dividing cells broadly, it also affects some healthy cells — explaining its well-known side effects. It can be given in multiple ways, in repeated cycles, and with different goals: to cure, to prepare for surgery, to clean up after surgery, or simply to extend and improve a patient's life when a full cure is not possible. It remains one of the most widely used and important tools in cancer medicine, often combined with surgery, radiation, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy.
2759: Chenille (noun) refers to two closely related things: a type of yarn and the fabric made from that yarn. Both share the same name. Understanding the yarn first makes the fabric easy to grasp.

Chenille yarn is a special kind of thread that looks and feels like a fuzzy caterpillar. Here's what makes it unique:

At its center, there are two thin core threads twisted tightly together. During manufacturing, tiny soft fibers — called the pile — get caught and locked between these twisting core threads. These fibers stick out in all directions around the core, perpendicular to it, like the bristles of a bottle brush or the legs of a caterpillar.The result is a yarn that is exceptionally soft, thick, and plush — much fuzzier and more textured than ordinary smooth yarn.

When chenille yarn is woven or knitted into fabric, the pile fibers cover the entire surface, giving the fabric a velvety, soft, almost furry feel. The surface has a distinctive richness and depth that flat fabrics don't have. Running your hand over it feels like stroking something gentle and cushiony.

The pile fibers in chenille can be made from many different materials:

  • Cotton — soft, breathable, casual; used for robes, bath mats, blankets
  • Rayon — gives chenille a beautiful silky sheen; used for upholstery and throws
  • Acrylic or polyester — affordable, durable, widely used in modern blankets and furniture fabric
  • Wool — warm and natural; used in throws and clothing
  • Silk — rare and very luxurious

The material determines the look, feel, durability, and price of the final product.

One of the most distinctive things about chenille is that its pile can be brushed or pushed in different directions. When the pile lies one way, light reflects off it and it looks lighter. Brush it the other way, and it looks darker. This means you can literally trace patterns on chenille with your hand — your touch leaves a visible mark.

This light-and-shadow effect when the pile is disturbed is called tracking (or sometimes "shading"), and it's considered a normal, natural characteristic of chenille — not a defect.

Chenille is used very widely, especially anywhere softness and comfort are the goal:

  • Furniture upholstery — sofas, armchairs, ottomans; chenille is one of the most popular upholstery fabrics because it's soft, warm, and comfortable to sit on
  • Throws and blankets — the fuzzy, plush blankets draped over sofas are very often chenille
  • Bedspreads and comforters — the classic "tufted bedspread" (common in mid-20th-century American homes) was typically chenille
  • Sweaters and clothing — chenille knit sweaters have a cozy, plush feel; scarves too
  • Rugs — especially bath mats and decorative area rugs
  • Cushion and pillow covers
  • Craft pipe cleaners — the fuzzy, bendable sticks used in arts and crafts are actually a form of chenille: a wire core with chenille fibers twisted around it. This is why they are technically called chenille stems.
Things to know about chenille's behavior

Chenille has some quirks worth understanding:

  • Shedding — New chenille items often shed loose pile fibers, especially when new. This is normal and usually reduces over time.
  • Crushing — If something heavy sits on chenille for a long time, the pile can flatten. Gently brushing it can restore it.
  • Delicate pile — The pile fibers are attached at one point, not woven deeply through. This means very rough use or frequent friction in the same spot can wear it down, causing thin or bald-looking patches over time.
  • Care — Most chenille items should be washed gently (cold water, gentle cycle, no aggressive wringing) to preserve the pile. Many upholstery chenilles are dry-clean only.
  • Warmth — Because of its thick, textured surface that traps air, chenille is a warm fabric, which is why it's so popular for blankets and winter clothing.
The key idea to hold on to

Think of a fuzzy caterpillar. That image captures chenille perfectly. Whether you encounter the word referring to yarn in a craft store, fabric in a furniture showroom, a soft blanket, or a cozy sweater — the defining trait is always the same: a core with short fibers sticking out all around it, creating an exceptionally soft, thick, plush, velvety texture.
